_: Nancy Rubins, 'Monochrome for Austin', 2015 — the largest work in the Landmarks collection, at the north-west corner of 24th and Speedway. Seventy aluminium canoes and small boats cantilevered off a stainless armature. EVERY number below carries the pixel or the publication it came from. See docs/real-art.md for the working.
name: Monochrome for Austin
atSource: landmarks.utexas.edu/artwork/monochrome-austin, 'GPS: 30.287462, -97.737132'. data/art.geojson's parts centre on -97.7370979, 30.2874649 (a buffered OSM node) — 3.4 m away. `atFromData` keeps the piece where its label and footprint already are.

dims.source: '600 x 642 x 492 inches' — landmarks.utexas.edu/artwork/monochrome-austin. 600 in = 15.24 m, 642 in = 16.31 m, 492 in = 12.50 m. scripts/bake_art.py's DIMS has the width at 15.85 m from a secondary source; 642 in off Landmarks' own object label is 16.31 m and is what this file uses.

hulls.countSource: 'a monumental sculpture consisting of 70 aluminum canoes and small boats' — landmarks.utexas.edu/artwork/monochrome-austin.
hulls.dimSource: MEASURED against the published height in Landmarks' elevation photograph (photo Paul Bardagjy, gallery image '29_rubins_monochromeforaustin'): the frame runs 750 px from the plinth's base to the topmost hull tip for the published 15.24 m, i.e. 49.2 px/m. Individual hulls measure 215-275 px long (4.4-5.6 m) and 35-42 px in the beam (0.71-0.85 m). Canoe and small-boat dimensions, which is what the object label says they are.
hulls.profileSource: As fractions of hull length, applied to |u|^kickPow (see ART3D.prof in js/slopes-art.js), so the keel and the gunwale are STRAIGHT down the middle and turn up over the last sixth. MEASURED in Landmarks' own detail frame (photo Paul Bardagjy): the gunwale of the foremost hull is a straight line for four fifths of its length and sweeps up only at the tips, and the beam is still nearly full at mid-length. LOOK-FIX 2: this file's first pass ran both on u^2, which bends the whole hull, and seventy bent hulls radiating outward read as a wheel of scythes rather than a tangle of boats. Depth also raised 0.42 -> 0.46: at 0.42 with the old taper most of the length was too thin to have any volume.

cloud.envelopeSource: MEASURED in the same elevation photograph at 49.2 px/m: the mass runs from y=1100 px (its lowest hull, 2.4 m above grade, just clear of the plinth head) to y=505 px (15.24 m), so its centre sits 8.8 m up and its vertical semi-axis is 6.05 m; it spans 840 px = 17.1 m across that face against the published 16.31 m, so semiX 8.15 m. semiY is the published 12.50 m depth halved. The envelope is where the TIPS reach, not where the centres sit — see `core`.
cloud.radialSource: THE RULE THE OLD RECIPE MISSED, and it is the whole silhouette. In every photograph each hull's long axis points OUTWARD FROM THE CORE: the inner end is buried in the mass and the pointed end juts clear of it, so the work reads as a burst of boats. scripts/bake_art.py drew each hull at an INDEPENDENT random heading (`a = 2*pi*hash01('hull', ...)`), uncorrelated with where the hull sat, and an uncorrelated cloud of sticks is a lump however many of them there are. 0.86 is how far each hull is turned from its own random heading onto the radial one: 1.0 is a perfect sea urchin, 0 is the old bake. LOOK-FIX 3: back up to 0.86 now that the lattice and `jitter` carry the tangle — the randomness no longer has to do two jobs at once.
cloud.floorSource: No hull comes below this. MEASURED: the lowest hull in the elevation photograph sits at y=1100 px, 2.4 m above grade, just clear of the plinth head at 2.34 m. 2.2 m leaves the cantilever reading without a hull tip through the pavement.
cloud.innerSource: LOOK-FIX 3, and it replaced two tuned parameters with the physical rule. Every hull is bolted to a central armature, so its INNER END sits near the core and its pointed end radiates: place the inner end at innerMin..innerMax metres from the core and the hull's own length carries the tip to innerMax + lenMax = 2.70 + 5.60 = 8.30 m, which is the 8.15 m semi-axis measured off the elevation photograph. The dense middle and the spiky outline both fall out of that, so the outward `core` bias and the nine bolted-on `spikes` the first two passes needed are both gone, and the hull count is now exactly the published 70.
cloud.jitterSource: Radians. Directions come off a FIBONACCI LATTICE over the 70 hulls rather than a hash, because seventy independently hashed directions on a sphere CLUMP: the first pass here had a comb of near-parallel hulls down one side and a hole on the other, which is what independent sampling looks like and is not what the photographs show. The lattice covers every direction evenly; this jitter puts the tangle back.

plinth.source: MEASURED in the elevation photograph at 49.2 px/m: the concrete pier is 40 px wide (0.81 m) and runs 115 px from grade to its head (2.34 m). It is strikingly small under a 16 m mass, and that contrast is most of why the work reads as cantilevered.

mast.source: The stainless yoke and armature stub above the plinth head, up into the underside of the cloud; 3.6 m is where the photographs' lowest hulls close over it. Mostly hidden by the time the cloud is drawn, which is correct — 'draws its support from a steel armature and intertwining cables' (Landmarks), and the armature is not what you see.

cables.source: 'intertwining cables' — Landmarks. A stainless cable on this piece is about 20 mm and would be sub-pixel at every zoom this app flies at, so it is DRAWN at 0.09 m: the same deliberate over-width as bake_tower.py's clock dial (3.05 m drawn for a true 3.66 m) and SLOPES_ROOFS.lines.ridge (1.0 m drawn for a true 0.4 m). The count is the number that reads against the sky in the elevation photograph, not a survey.
cables.maxSource: A tie longer than this is not drawn. The cables in the photographs are short ties inside the tangle; a long straight run across the mass reads as a suspension bridge, which is what the first pass here drew.

material.source: SAMPLED, and it corrects a real error. Median RGB of hull faces in Landmarks' photographs: lit #5e6166 and #77716f, shaded #423c3b, against a concrete plinth in the same frame at #cac2bc. The boats read at about HALF the luminance of concrete — weathered aluminium against a bright sky, not mill finish. scripts/bake_art.py painted them 'alum' #b9bec6 and 'mirror' #cdd8e0, which is a cloud of silver foil. Day is the diffuse reading brought onto the app's own concrete reference (js/props.js ARTMAT 'limest' #ded7c6 at 222 luma x 0.5). One hull in four takes the brighter tone, because the light-and-dark scatter across the mass is what makes seventy overlapping shells read as seventy objects rather than one. LOOK-FIX 1: day lifted one step from #7c8086 to #8a8e94 and the bright share from one in four to one in three. Against a bright pavement in the app the sampled tone read as dark as the tree trunks beside it; the photographs' hulls are dark against SKY, which is a different contrast problem from the one this scene has. LOOK-FIX 2: the bright tone lifted again to #bcc2c8 — the reference's sunlit hulls against blue sky are near-white, and the piece's whole read is the scatter between those and the shaded ones. LOOK-FIX 4: the cockpit tone lifted from #4a4e54 to #6a6e74. A canoe's interior in daylight is a mid-grey with light down one side of it, not a black slot, and at the old value every hull seen from above was a dark gash — the exact opposite of the reference nadir, where the cluster is a burst of BRIGHT pointed shapes (Esri World Imagery z21, 0.0645 m/px, over Landmarks' published 30.287462,-97.737132).
material.plinthSource: SAMPLED off the plinth in the same photograph: (202,194,188).
material.steelSource: js/props.js ARTMAT 'steel', unchanged — the armature and cables keep the palette's own steel.
